prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It has arrived—the long rag rug multiply folded. On top, one alien hair. I put my face to the folds and smell despair palpable as salt air in all those rooms and houses, small and smug— enclosures I passed through on my way where? Whoever did the weaving appears old in my mind’s eye. I can’t make out her face, can only conjure up the faintest trace of an abstracted grace, clack of the loom. Does she know they’ll be sold these precious things, in some unheard-of place? I perch her on a hill, precariously beyond the reach of waves’ daily boom. Sun blazes overhead, but her dim room (no bigger than the loom) is proof against the violence of the sky From it I further spin what I once called my home: Endless horizons fading into haze, the mornings dawn came up so rosy clear; snails in the garden, sheep bells everywhere, the brightness of the air, terraces, valleys organizing space and time’s cessation. So this package here I’m now unwrapping, in New York, today (rugs like rainbows, woven with a grace my strands of language barely can express; dishrags of dailiness dispersed and recombined and freshly gay) comes to me imbued with images, slowly and faithfully across the water, across the world. It represents a time I myself snipped and recombined as rhyme as soon as I went home, if that is where I am. These rugs recover the sense of stepping twice into a single river.

The speaker unwraps a handmade rag rug in New York, using its textures, scent, and imagined weaver to reconstruct memories of a distant former home. Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whoever, Does, Sun

outputs.L1:
It has arrived—the long rag rug, multiply folded. On top lies a single alien hair. I press my face to the folds and smell despair, palpable as salt air in all those rooms and houses, small and smug—the enclosures I passed through on my way where?

Whoever did the weaving appears old in my mind’s eye. I cannot make out her face; I can conjure only the faintest trace of an abstracted grace, the clack of the loom. Does she know that these precious things will be sold in some unheard-of place? I perch her on a hill, precariously beyond the reach of the waves’ daily boom. The sun blazes overhead, but her dim room—no bigger than the loom—is proof against the violence of the sky.

From it, I spin further what I once called my home: endless horizons fading into haze; the morning’s dawn rising rosy and clear; snails in the garden; sheep bells everywhere; the brightness of the air; terraces and valleys organizing space; and time’s cessation.

And so this package, which I am unwrapping here in New York today—rugs like rainbows, woven with a grace my strands of language can barely express; dishrags of dailiness dispersed, recombined, and freshly gay—comes to me imbued with images, slowly and faithfully, across the water and across the world. It represents a time I myself snipped and recombined as rhyme as soon as I went home, if that is where I am. These rugs recover the sense of stepping twice into a single river.
outputs.L2:
At last it is here: the long rag rug, folded again and again. A single unfamiliar hair rests on its surface. I press my face into the layers and breathe in a desolation as tangible as ocean salt, recalling all the tidy, self-satisfied little rooms and houses I moved through—though toward what destination?

In my imagination, the woman who wove it is elderly. Her features remain indistinct; I can summon only a shadow of her distant elegance and the steady clatter of the loom. Does she realize that these treasured objects will be sold somewhere she has never heard of? I picture her poised uncertainly on a hill above the everyday thunder of the waves. The sun burns fiercely, yet her dark chamber, scarcely larger than the loom itself, shelters her from the sky’s brutality.

From that room, my mind continues weaving what I once understood as home: limitless horizons dissolving into mist; dawn arriving in flawless shades of pink; snails among the garden plants; sheep bells sounding on every side; luminous air; terraces and valleys arranging the landscape, while time seems to stop.

And so, as I open this parcel in New York today, the rugs reach me saturated with visions, having traveled patiently and steadily over the sea and around the globe. They are rainbowlike creations, fashioned with an artistry my threads of speech can hardly convey—ordinary scraps of domestic life separated, rearranged, and made newly joyful. They embody a past that I, too, cut apart and reassembled into rhyme as soon as I returned home, assuming this place can be called home. Through these rugs, I regain the feeling that it is possible to enter the same river twice.
outputs.L3:
The arrival of the folded rag rug evokes in the speaker a palpable sense of despair, while also awakening memories of the many enclosed homes to which such an object might belong. Looking at it, the speaker imagines the elderly woman who wove it and wonders whether she realizes that her precious handiwork will eventually be sold in a distant and unfamiliar place. In the speaker’s imagination, the weaver works in a small room that offers shelter and comfort from the harsh natural world outside.

When the rug is finally unwrapped in New York, it becomes more than a household object. Its colors and textures summon vivid memories of home: bright mornings, flourishing gardens, the sound of bells around the necks of sheep, sunlit terraces, and deep valleys. Made from ordinary scraps of material, the rug demonstrates the power of human creativity to transform what is humble or discarded into something beautiful and enduring. At the same time, it reconnects the speaker with a distant past—a past that can no longer be recovered exactly as it was, but that has been preserved and reshaped through memory, imagination, and language.
outputs.L4:
In New York, far from the place once known as home, the speaker unwraps a handmade rag rug. The moment becomes much more than the opening of a package. As the rug unfolds, its rough textures, familiar colors, and lingering scent awaken memories that distance and displacement have not erased. The speaker studies the strips of reused cloth and imagines the hands of the woman who wove them, patiently turning worn fragments into a new and coherent pattern. Through this imagined connection with the weaver, the rug becomes a bridge between the speaker’s present life and the distant world left behind.

Each scrap of fabric seems to carry part of an earlier existence: traces of clothing, domestic routines, family histories, and everyday labor. Although these materials have been cut apart and rearranged, they have not lost their past. Instead, their transformation resembles the work of memory itself. Memory cannot restore a former home exactly as it was, but it can gather scattered details and reassemble them into something that remains emotionally true. The rug therefore embodies both rupture and continuity. Its pieces have been separated from their original uses, just as the speaker has been separated from home, yet they survive within a different form.

By bringing these fragments together, the weaver creates beauty out of what might otherwise have been discarded. Her craft suggests that loss does not have to result in complete disappearance. What has been broken, worn, or displaced can be preserved through acts of imagination and making. As the speaker touches and smells the rug, the past becomes almost physically present. Home is no longer merely a distant location; it is experienced through the senses and reconstructed in the mind.

The rug ultimately serves as a symbol of art’s power to make return possible without denying the reality of exile. The speaker cannot literally recover the former home or step back into an unchanged past. Nevertheless, the woven object offers another kind of return: a return through memory, touch, inherited labor, and creative transformation. Like the rug, belonging can be remade from fragments. The result is not identical to what existed before, but it is durable and meaningful. Through the rug, the speaker discovers that displacement may alter one’s relationship to home, yet it cannot entirely destroy the desire or capacity to belong.
outputs.L5:
**Whoever Does the Sun Follow?**

Whoever wakes before the dawn  
will hear the silence break.  
Does the sky remember night  
when morning starts to wake?

The Sun climbs over distant hills,  
painting gold on everyone.  
Whoever dares to follow hope  
will always find the Sun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about receiving a handwoven rag rug in New York and being transported back to a former Mediterranean home, exploring memory, exile, craft, and the impossibility of returning.
counterfactuals.output:
The rug arrived in New York folded into a square, tied with twine, smelling faintly of wool, dust, and some weather I could not name. When I opened it, the room altered. The radiator’s iron breath became the rasp of cicadas; sirens thinned into gull-cries. Beneath my hands, strips of old cloth crossed and recrossed: indigo, rust, pomegranate, the pale green of shutters blistered by salt.

Someone had torn dresses, aprons, shirts no longer worn, and given them another grammar. The loom had gathered what time discarded and persuaded it to hold. I traced a blue thread and found the sea. I traced a white one and found the courtyard at noon, its stones too bright to look at. In a red strand, my mother shook crumbs from a tablecloth; in yellow, lemons waited in a bowl, small suns with bitter skins.

I laid the rug beside the window, twenty floors above a street glossed with rain. Taxis passed like restless lanterns. Yet under my bare feet the old house opened: the long corridor, the chipped basin, the balcony where laundry filled with wind and became the sails of departing ships. For one breath I stood there again, not as I am, but as the person who had not yet left.

This is the mercy of craft: it makes a threshold from remnants. This is its cruelty: the threshold does not lead back.

The house may belong to strangers now, or to ivy, or to the patient salt. The fig tree may have split the wall. The neighbors may have forgotten our names. Even if I returned, carrying the key I still keep in a drawer, the lock would refuse me—or worse, it would open, and nothing inside would recognize my face.

So I remain in New York, where winter climbs the glass and the river carries its dark cargo toward the harbor. Each morning I step onto the woven colors. Exile, too, is made this way: strip by strip, loss crossing habit, longing crossing distance, until what cannot be mended becomes something we can stand upon.

The rug does not bring me home. It teaches the floor to remember.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ekphrastic monologue in the voice of an expatriate unwrapping a handmade rug. Include an unknown weaver, sea imagery, village landscapes, and a meditation on whether “home” can be recovered through art.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Carpet Keeps**

Easy—here, take the cord. It has crossed three borders knotted around itself, gathering the smell of warehouses, rain, and the hands of men who never asked what it contained.

There.

Already the room changes.

The rug opens slowly, as if waking beneath my fingers. First a strip of blue—not the blue of this northern harbor, all iron and gull-cry, but the blue of the sea below my mother’s house, where noon shattered into silver scales. Then red: pomegranate skin, roof tile, the dark seam of earth where the plow had passed. And green, though no green in nature ever held so still.

Who made you?

The dealer said only: a woman from an inland village. He could not remember which village, or else he thought I would not know the difference. Perhaps you sat at a loom beside an open door. Perhaps goats moved like loose stones along the hill, and smoke rose from the bread ovens. Perhaps, while your hands traveled—under, over, under—you heard a child reciting lessons, a bucket striking the lip of a well, the sea breathing beyond the terraces.

Or perhaps I invent all this because I need your hands to have known my world.

Here, in the center: a house no bigger than my thumbnail. White walls, two black windows, a path descending through cypress trees. Is it your house? Mine? No house I knew had such perfect walls. Ours leaned into the wind. Its shutters would not close in winter, and salt bloomed on the hinges. Yet when I look at this woven house, I can hear my father clearing his throat in the courtyard. I can smell lemons cut open on a plate.

That is art’s trick, perhaps: not to return what was lost, but to give loss a body.

You have knotted a village along the border—little roofs, little fields, a shepherd repeated four times as if walking around the world. Beyond him, waves. Strange waves for an inland weaver: hooked white crests, dark fish, a boat with no sail. Did someone tell you the sea? Did you remember it from childhood? Or is this not water at all, but mountains turned upside down?

I have lived away so long that my own memories have begun to resemble patterns. The fountain, the fig tree, the road to the chapel—I repeat them until they become symbols, neat and durable, unlike the actual things. The fountain has cracked. The fig tree was cut down. The road is paved now and leads to a hotel whose windows glare at the bay.

Still, I kneel here, smoothing the corners.

If I lay you in this rented room, will the walls learn my language? Will the radiator’s knocking become cicadas? Will these gray windows fill with sun? Can a woven sea carry me back across the real one?

No. I know better.

Home is not hidden in the wool like a message. I cannot unroll it intact. Whatever country I left has gone on without me, changing its face, forgetting my footsteps. And I have changed too. Even if I returned, I would arrive as a guest carrying an old map.

But look—your blue reaches the red field. The village holds. The boat does not sink.

Unknown woman, wherever you are, you made no portrait of my childhood. You did not know my mother’s house, my father’s voice, the harbor at dusk. Yet your hands left openings where my dead could enter. You tied distance into beauty. You made a place that never existed, and because it never existed, it cannot be destroyed.

Perhaps that is the only home art can recover: not the house, not the country, not the life before leaving, but the shape our longing makes around them.

I will place the rug where morning falls.

Tomorrow I will step onto it barefoot. Beneath me, the small boat will cross its endless sea. The shepherd will circle the village. Smoke will rise without vanishing. And for one moment—not returned, not forgiven, but held—I will stand inside the patient country of your hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, modernist prose poem centered on a package arriving from overseas. The object inside should evoke domestic labor, nostalgia, displacement, and Heraclitus’s idea that one cannot step into the same river twice.
counterfactuals.output: The package arrived salted by three seas, its corners crushed into the grammar of distance. Inside: my mother’s linen apron, yellowed at the throat, its pockets furred with flour, lint, one black seed from a country whose name the customs clerk had misspelled. I lifted it and the kitchen opened—not the kitchen, never the kitchen, but its smoke-double: copper pot, split soap, onions shining under the knife, her hands reddened by water, always entering and leaving the basin. What is a home but labor remembering itself in objects? The hem carried her small corrections, blue stitches crossing white cloth like bridges over a river already elsewhere. I tied it around my waist. It did not fit. Outside, rain combed the foreign windows; inside, the dead clock resumed its ticking. I thought: this flour is not flour, this stain not the afternoon when she leaned over the stove and called me by the childhood name I have since translated out of use. Yet the cloth warmed against me, obedient as an old servant, and for one breath I stood where she had stood, though Heraclitus, severe at the sink, turned on the tap: no hand enters the same water twice, no exile unwraps the country that was sent. The apron smelled of iron, lavender, and passage. I washed it. The water clouded, carrying home away from home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a writer in New York receives several colorful rag rugs from a place where they once lived. Describe the rugs’ textures and smells, invent the elderly woman who wove them, and let the unwrapping trigger fragmented memories of terraces, sheep bells, gardens, and bright coastal air.
counterfactuals.output:
The parcel arrived in New York bound with blue twine, its corners softened by the long journey. When I cut it open, the rugs rose out of the paper as if they had been holding their breath.

They were striped in pomegranate, indigo, saffron, and the green of crushed olive leaves. Their surfaces were rough but not harsh: ridges of old cotton dresses, wool skirts, flour sacks, and ribbons of cloth twisted tight by patient fingers. Loose threads tickled my wrists. Dust lifted from them—not city dust, but the dry, sun-warmed smell of stone houses, lanolin, woodsmoke, lavender shut in a drawer. One rug carried a faint sweetness, like figs stored through winter; another smelled sharply of goat soap and the sea.

I imagined their maker as Kyria Eleni, eighty-six, small and square-backed, with silver hair braided around her head. She would weave beside a low window, her feet in black slippers, her hands knuckled and quick. She saved every scrap. This red was her daughter’s wedding blouse, she would say. This blue came from a dead fisherman’s shirt. She spoke to the loom when no one else was there, scolding it, praising it, asking it to remember.

I spread the rugs across my apartment floor. Outside, a bus exhaled at the curb. Sirens opened and closed in the distance. But the colors broke something loose.

A terrace at noon.

White steps descending between walls.

Sheep bells moving somewhere beyond the ridge—first one, then many, an uneven silver music.

A garden behind rusted wire: tomatoes split with heat, basil bruised under a thumb, bees staggering through yellow flowers.

Then nothing.

Then the blue door of the house where I had slept. A cracked basin. Wet sheets snapping on a line. A woman calling from below, her words carried upward and torn apart by wind.

I pressed my face to the largest rug.

Bright air returned—the coastal air that made every edge distinct: roof tiles, cypress needles, the black seam of a boat on the water. The sea itself was hidden, but light from it flashed everywhere, on windows, on lizards, on the pale undersides of leaves.

For a moment my New York room tilted into that lost country. The fire escape became a balcony. Radiator knocks became bells. Between the buildings, in a narrow blade of winter sky, I saw the impossible summer brightness.

Then the room settled.

The rugs remained under my hands, stubborn and vivid, woven from clothes no one wore anymore, holding dust from roads I had almost forgotten.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph literary meditation in ornate, sensory language about weaving and recollection. Draw parallels between scraps becoming a rug and lived experience becoming poetry, ending with the paradoxical feeling of stepping twice into the same river.
counterfactuals.output: At the loom, memory loosens its hoard: a blue shred smelling faintly of cedar, a ribbon worn soft by a child’s wrist, the wine-dark hem of a dress once lifted through summer dust; beneath the patient shuttle, these remnants cross and clasp, surrendering their solitude to pattern, until loss itself grows warm underfoot. So lived hours enter the narrow frame of poetry—frayed mornings, bright quarrels, the salt of farewells, the small gold lint of joy—each drawn taut, broken, braided with another, not restored to what it was but transfigured into something the hands can touch and the heart can inhabit. Recollection is such weaving: the past returns not as a road behind us, but as color under pressure, a woven current whose threads keep moving even after they are bound. And when I step upon the finished rug, feeling every vanished life rise softly through its knots, I know the strange tenderness of stepping twice into the same river—and finding both the river and myself changed, yet somehow, impossibly, the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
